title: Pica (disorder)
wiki_lead:
Pica ( PY-kə) is the psychologically compulsive craving or consumption of objects that are not normally intended to be consumed. It is classified as an eating disorder but can also be the result of an existing mental disorder. The ingested or craved substance may be biological, natural, or manmade. The term was drawn directly from the Latin word for the Eurasian magpie, a bird subject to much folklore regarding its opportunistic feeding behaviors.
According to the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 5th edition (DSM-5), pica as a standalone eating disorder must persist for more than one month at an age when eating such objects is considered developmentally inappropriate, not part of culturally sanctioned practice, and sufficiently severe to warrant clinical attention. Pica may lead to intoxication in children, which can result in an impairment of both physical and mental development. In addition, it can cause surgical emergencies due to intestinal obstructions, as well as more subtle symptoms such as nutritional deficiencies, particularly iron deficiency, as well as parasitosis. Pica has been linked to other mental disorders. Stressors such as psychological trauma, maternal deprivation, family issues, parental neglect, pregnancy, and a disorganized family structure are risk factors for pica.
Pica is most commonly seen in pregnant women, small children, and people who may have developmental disorders such as autism. Children eating painted plaster containing lead may develop brain damage from lead poisoning. A similar risk exists from eating soil near roads that existed before the phase-out of tetraethyllead or that were sprayed with oil (to settle dust) contaminated by toxic PCBs or dioxin. In addition to poisoning, a much greater risk exists of gastrointestinal obstruction or tearing in the stomach. Another risk of eating soil is the ingestion of animal feces and accompanying parasites. Cases of severe bacterial infections occurrence (leptospirosis) in patients diagnosed with pica have also been reported. Pica can also be found in animals such as dogs and cats.

Complications
Complications may occur due to the substance consumed. For example, lead poisoning may result from the ingestion of paint or paint-soaked plaster, hairballs may cause intestinal obstruction, and Toxoplasma or Toxocara infections may follow ingestion of feces or soil.

grok_lead: Pica is an eating disorder characterized by the persistent consumption of non-nutritive substances, such as dirt, clay, paper, or ice, for a period of at least one month at an age or developmental level where this behavior is inappropriate. Named after the Latin word for the Eurasian magpie ( Pica pica), a bird known for its indiscriminate gathering of objects, pica involves compulsive ingestion of items that provide no nutritional benefit and can range from harmless to life-threatening depending on the substances consumed. The disorder is classified in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-5-TR) as a feeding and eating disorder, distinct from normal exploratory behaviors in young children or culturally sanctioned practices. The primary symptom of pica is an intense craving and repeated eating of non-food items, which may lead to serious health complications including gastrointestinal obstructions, infections, nutritional deficiencies, or poisoning from toxins like lead in paint. While the exact causes remain unclear, pica is strongly associated with nutritional deficiencies, particularly iron and zinc, as well as psychosocial factors such as stress, neglect, or developmental disabilities; pica has been detected in up to 50% of individuals with iron deficiency anemia in Western countries. It is more prevalent in certain populations, including children aged 1-6 (with rates of 10-28% among those with intellectual disabilities or autism spectrum disorder), pregnant individuals (up to 27.8% prevalence), and people with conditions like sickle cell disease (34% prevalence). Diagnosis typically involves a thorough clinical history to confirm the behavior's persistence and exclusion of cultural or medical necessities, often supplemented by blood tests for deficiencies or imaging for complications. Treatment is multidisciplinary, emphasizing behavioral interventions like positive reinforcement to encourage appropriate eating habits (with recent studies showing at least 90% reduction in behaviors), alongside nutritional supplementation; in cases tied to iron deficiency, symptoms often resolve rapidlyâsometimes within daysâupon correction of the underlying anemia. Although pica frequently remits spontaneously in children and during pregnancy, untreated cases can result in severe sequelae, underscoring the importance of early intervention in at-risk groups.
